evaluation.positioning_hook: A lesbian hospital doctor hunts a blood plague in San Francisco and discovers the epidemic is a vampire sisterhood feeding on the city’s women.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a clean, easy-to-grasp horror engine: a mysterious blood disease, a hospital under siege, and a vampire reveal that escalates into a full nocturnal assault. The San Francisco setting, queer central relationship, and pulpy sexuality give it a distinct lane for genre buyers and late-night audiences.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands immediately in the opening microscope sequence and the terminal ward outbreak, then sharpens when Frost realizes the victims are all women and Rose is tied to the contagion. The story engine is legible: diagnose the plague, identify the carrier, and survive the vampire network.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Diana Frost carries the movie with a strong contradiction: physically formidable, clinically driven, and emotionally entangled with the woman at the center of the outbreak. Rose and Van Trapp add romantic and moral pressure, while Marsha gives the story a seductive antagonist with real screen presence.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a very specific blend of medical horror, queer melodrama, and vampire mythology, with a hospital administrator, a priest, and a talk-show reveal all feeding the same engine. The female-only infection pattern and the erotic charge around the vampire world give it a sharper identity than a standard bloodsucker story.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: It moves with strong forward pressure: outbreak, diagnosis, investigation, seduction, confrontation, then a full-scale siege and inferno. The second half especially keeps turning the screw with set pieces in the apartment, church, mission, and hospital ward.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script’s most memorable idea is the disease-as-vampirism reveal filtered through a women’s ward and a queer love triangle. That combination feels both familiar in genre terms and freshly organized around a specific social and sexual world.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: San Francisco is used well as a foggy, morally split city: hospital corridors, red-light streets, a Catholic church, elite hillside house, and a converted mission/hotel all contribute to a vivid nocturnal map. The institutional world of hospital politics and public media also gives the story a broader civic frame.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unmistakably lurid and heightened, with hard-edged dialogue, explicit sexuality, body horror, and melodramatic declarations all living in the same frame. It knows exactly what kind of movie it is and keeps leaning into that pulp-gothic register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the monster plot, the script suggests a story about shame, desire, betrayal, and the social policing of women’s sexuality. Frost, Rose, Van Trapp, and Marsha all carry emotional and symbolic weight that could support a richer dramatic reading.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The movie is anchored by a strong central triangle/quadrangle: Frost and Rose, Frost and Van Trapp, Rose and Marsha, with Van Trapp as the pragmatic ally caught in the middle. The supporting world is functional and colorful, though the core energy clearly lives in those central relationships.

casting_characteristics: Female lead in mid-30s with physicality and authority
One major male supporting role in his 40s-50s
Several nurses, orderlies, interns, and patients

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with recurring exterior city and street scenes
notable_requirements: Hospital ward, lab, cafeteria, office, and corridors
Lesbian bar and red-light district exteriors
Elite hillside residence with Jacuzzi and pool

technical.vfx_details: Bat-creature transformation, Marsha’s vampiric morphing, smoke/ectoplasm effects, blood effects, window smash/fall, burning car and sign sequence, television/news inserts
technical.sfx_needs: Heavy blood effects, practical creature makeup, prosthetic fangs, body impacts, glass breakage, fire effects, elevator violence

rights_flags.detail: Evian is specifically visible on the bottle label

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Theatrical genre, festival-to-platform, or premium streaming horror
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong midnight-movie and genre-fan appeal

strengths.what_it_means: The movie turns a medical mystery into a vampire outbreak, giving the story a clean commercial engine that is easy to pitch and easy to market.
strengths.evidence: The opening microscope diagnosis, the terminal ward outbreak, and the later Society of Vampirism reveal all build one escalating concept.

strengths.what_it_means: Diana Frost is a physically commanding, emotionally conflicted lead with star texture — a doctor who can fight, diagnose, and break under personal pressure.
strengths.evidence: She’s introduced as a powerfully built doctor, lifts weights, confronts the outbreak, and is emotionally destabilized by Rose and Marsha.

strengths.what_it_means: The Frost/Rose relationship gives the horror a distinctive emotional center and opens the script to audiences looking for queer genre material with real heat.
strengths.evidence: Their domestic scenes, jealousy, reconciliation, and betrayal are woven directly into the infection plot.

strengths.what_it_means: Marsha is a seductive, theatrical antagonist with a strong visual identity, which is exactly the kind of role that can attract a scene-stealing actor.
strengths.evidence: She appears through a personal ad, seduces Rose, dominates the final mission sequence, and leads a vampiress sisterhood.

strengths.what_it_means: The script is built around memorable genre moments that can sell trailers and audience word-of-mouth: the ward attack, the hospital elevator kill, the church blessing, and the burning car finale.
strengths.evidence: Multiple contained action sequences escalate the horror in visually distinct spaces.

strengths.what_it_means: Foggy San Francisco, the red-light district, Catholic spaces, and elite private interiors create a city that feels morally and visually specific.
strengths.evidence: The script repeatedly uses the bay fog, neon streets, church imagery, and hospital bureaucracy as part of the atmosphere.

strengths.what_it_means: This knows how to be pulpy without apology, which gives it a clear identity in the horror marketplace and a strong midnight-movie personality.
strengths.evidence: The dialogue is blunt and sexual, the violence is operatic, and the supernatural reveal is played with full melodramatic force.

whats_special.headline: This is a bold, highly marketable queer vampire horror with a medical-thriller spine and a pulpy, midnight-movie attitude. Diana Frost is the kind of physically formidable, emotionally compromised lead that can anchor a cult favorite, while Marsha and the vampiress reveal give the movie a villain world with real franchise energy.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Diana Frost
lead_characters.hook: A hard-driving hospital doctor with a fighter’s body and a clinician’s mind, Diana is all control on the surface and all fracture underneath. She’s competent in crisis, blunt in conversation, and emotionally exposed where Rose is concerned. What makes her specific is the collision of authority and vulnerability: she can diagnose a plague, throw a punch, and still be undone by jealousy, loyalty, and desire.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a showcase role for an actor who wants to play command, erotic tension, and emotional collapse in one package. The part has the physical authority of a genre heroine and the romantic damage of a noir lead, with strong scenes of confrontation, confession, and action. It lives in the same performance space as Sigourney Weaver in Alien and Jodie Foster in The Silence of the Lambs in terms of intelligence under pressure, while also giving the actor a sex-forward, emotionally charged edge.

lead_characters.name: Rose
lead_characters.demographics: Female · late 20s to mid-30s · feminine, vulnerable, sensual
lead_characters.hook: Rose is the emotional hinge of the story: tender, conflicted, and pulled between the life she has with Frost and the dangerous pull of Marsha. She reads as soft-spoken but not passive, with a private life that carries real erotic charge and real shame. Her specificity comes from the way the script frames her as both beloved partner and potential vector of catastrophe.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a deeply playable role for an actor who can carry longing, secrecy, and vulnerability without losing sensuality. The part offers intimate scenes, romantic history, and the chance to become the emotional center of a horror narrative. It has the kind of tragic-romantic energy that can recall performances like Gena Rowlands in A Woman Under the Influence or Julianne Moore in Safe, where interior distress becomes the engine of the film.

lead_characters.name: Eldon Van Trapp
lead_characters.hook: The hospital administrator who looks like a civilized authority figure but gradually reveals a taste for danger, irony, and moral compromise. He’s witty, worldly, and unexpectedly game, which makes him the perfect ally when the story turns supernatural. He functions as both institutional power and comic-relief pressure valve, but he also becomes the movie’s most surprising survivalist.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a delicious supporting-lead part for an actor who can play charm, vanity, and panic in equal measure. The role gets sharp dialogue, a strong relationship with Frost, and a full transformation from bureaucrat to battlefield survivor. It has the kind of arc that lets an actor pivot from smooth authority to frantic physical comedy and horror, in the vein of performances like Jeff Goldblum in The Fly or John Goodman in genre mode.

lead_characters.name: Marsha Valadimar
lead_characters.hook: Marsha is the story’s erotic predator: elegant, commanding, and openly hungry for power. She enters through seduction, speaks like someone used to getting her way, and then reveals a full supernatural authority that makes her feel larger than the room. She’s not just a villain; she’s a fantasy of appetite and control with a cult-leader aura.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a prime villain role for an actor who wants to dominate the frame. The part offers seduction, menace, transformation, and a final-act escalation into full monster iconography. It has the kind of theatrical, scene-stealing energy that can sit in the same lane as performances like Catherine Deneuve in The Hunger or Jessica Lange in American Horror Story-style villainy.

considerations.detail: The story is built for a contained horror budget with a few larger set pieces: hospital interiors, apartment scenes, church sequences, and a finale that concentrates the spectacle into a handful of effects-driven moments.
The movie benefits from practical blood work, prosthetics, creature makeup, and selective VFX for transformations, smoke, and burning effects.
The project is especially dependent on a strong lead actress with physical presence and a second actress who can play seductive menace with authority.
The material sits naturally with adult horror audiences, queer genre viewers, and fans of erotic supernatural pulp.
The script leans into blood, sexuality, profanity, and body horror, which places it firmly in mature-rated territory.
San Francisco’s fog, neon nightlife, and Catholic imagery are doing real atmospheric work and give the movie a recognizable visual identity.
